The paper proposes decentralized stealth attack constructions that minimize mutual information I(X^n; Y^m_A) between state variables and measurements.
Attacks are formulated as random Gaussian distributions with zero mean and covariance matrix Σ_AA to minimize detection probability.
The observation model is linearized as Y^m = Hx + Z^m, where H is the Jacobian of the acquisition function.
State variables are modeled as X^n ~ N(0, Σ_XX) following a multivariate Gaussian distribution.
Measurements without attack follow Y^m ~ N(0, Σ_YY) where Σ_YY = HΣ_XX H^T + σ²I_m.
Under attack, measurements become Y^m_A = HX^n + Z^m + A^m with A^m ~ N(0, Σ_AA).
The independence assumption allows attackers to operate without communication: P_A^m = ∏^m_{i=1} P_A_i.
Each attacker i can only compromise measurement i, with A^m_i = A_i ⊗ e_i using the Kronecker product.
The global mutual information is I(X^n; Y^m_A) = (1/2) log(|Σ_YY + Σ_AA| / |σ²I_m + Σ_AA|).
The global KL divergence is D(P_Y^m_A || P_Y^m) = (1/2) log(|Σ_YY| / |Σ_YY_A|) + tr(Σ^{-1}_YY Σ_AA).
Joint detection uses a likelihood ratio test comparing P_Y^m (normal) versus P_Y^m_A (attacked).
Local detection tests individual measurements Y_i against hypotheses H_0: Y_i ~ N(0, e^T_i Σ_YY e_i) and H_1: Y_i ~ N(0, e^T_i Σ_YY e_i + v_i).
The decentralized attack construction is formulated as a potential game with convex potential functions.
The Nash Equilibrium of the proposed games is proven to be unique.
Three different potential games are proposed based on different degrees of attacker knowledge and coordination.
Best response dynamics are proposed as a practical method to achieve the Nash Equilibrium.
The paper evaluates performance on IEEE test systems to demonstrate feasibility of decentralized attacks.
Attackers use the cost function φ_i: R^m → R to determine optimal attack vectors A^m_i.
The Gaussian assumption for attacks minimizes mutual information for a fixed covariance matrix.
The zero mean assumption for attacks is justified because mutual information does not depend on the mean.
The paper addresses both global disruption (system-wide) and local detection (individual measurements).
Stealth is achieved by constraining the KL divergence between attacked and normal measurement distributions.
The framework assumes attackers have access to historical data to estimate the statistical structure of the CPS.
The paper demonstrates that game-theoretic techniques can describe coordination requirements for optimal decentralized attacks.
Cyber-physical systems are characterized by distributed and dynamic interactions between computational and physical components.
